message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%. CORRECTION: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.
F2. [misreport] The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%. CORRECTION: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.
F3. [method] Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June. CORRECTION: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.
F4. [inference] Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range. CORRECTION: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

EXTENSIONS:
- Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
- Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
- Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

FINAL VERSION:
# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

## Summary

The new CDN made the site much faster. Median page load time fell by about a third, and the slowest page loads improved by a similar proportion.

The rise in conversion over the same period cannot be credited to the CDN. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, from 2.50% to 2.70%. In the same calendar weeks last year it also rose by 0.2 points (2.4% to 2.6%), when nothing on the site changed. The summer ranges launched on 1 June in both years. After allowing for that seasonal lift, the best estimate of the CDN's effect on conversion is about zero. This holds whether the seasonal lift is treated as a fixed number of points or as a proportion. The estimate is imprecise, though, and a moderate effect in either direction cannot be ruled out.

These data cannot tell us what a faster site is worth. That needs a controlled test.

## Speed

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

Load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views, so they reflect what customers experienced on their own devices and connections. The slowest page loads improved slightly more than the typical one in relative terms. Half of page loads now complete within 2.1 seconds, and 95% within 4.8 seconds.

The improvement is large, and it started when the migration happened. Two caveats apply:

- **Content.** The summer launch changed page content and image weight, which could move load times either way.
- **Mix.** These are aggregate figures. If the summer launch shifted the traffic mix, for example towards more mobile visits or more product-page views, the aggregate would move even if no individual page got faster.

Even so, neither a content change nor a shift in mix is likely to cut load times by a third at both the median and the 95th percentile. Higher seasonal traffic would, if anything, tend to slow the site. The CDN is very likely the main cause of the speed gain. A breakdown by device, page type and region (next step 4) would confirm that the improvement is like for like.

## Engagement and volume

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% |
| Orders per day | ~357 | ~405 | +13% |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 points (−8% relative) |

Bounce rate is the share of sessions that view only one page. Its fall could come from a faster site, or from the summer launch giving visitors more reasons to browse. We do not have last year's bounce rate for the same weeks, so we cannot separate the two.

The 5% rise in sessions may also have more than one cause:

- It could be seasonal.
- It could include some search traffic gained from faster pages.
- It could partly reflect measurement (see "Other variation" below).

Last year's session counts would show how much of the rise is normal for the season.

## Conversion

| | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| This year (new CDN from 1 June) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 points |
| Last year (no site changes) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 points |
| **Difference (estimated CDN effect)** | | | **≈ 0 points** |

In relative terms the seasonal lift was about 8% in both years: 8.3% last year (0.2 ÷ 2.4) and 8.0% this year (0.2 ÷ 2.5). The summer range launch alone is enough to explain all of this year's increase.

The conclusion does not depend on how the seasonal lift is modelled:

- **As a fixed lift in points:** last year's +0.2 points leaves a CDN effect of about 0.
- **As a proportional lift:** last year's +8.3% applied to this May's 2.50% predicts 2.71% for June. The observed rate was 2.70%, which leaves a CDN effect of about −0.01 points. That is still zero.

The CDN was the only *site* change in the period, but it was not the only change. The summer launch happened on the same day, and a simple before/after comparison cannot separate the two.

**Precision.** The estimate of about zero is uncertain, for four reasons:

- **Sampling error this year.** Two weeks of data per period is short. Treating sessions as independent, the 95% interval on this year's 0.2-point rise is about ±0.1 points.
- **Sampling error in the comparison.** Comparing against last year adds last year's sampling error. If last year had similar traffic, the interval on the CDN effect widens to roughly ±0.15 points or more. The exact figure needs last year's session counts.
- **Rounding.** Last year's rates are given to one decimal place, so last year's lift could be anywhere from about 0.1 to 0.3 points. Rounding alone leaves the CDN effect anywhere from about −0.1 to +0.1 points.
- **Other variation.** Three further sources add uncertainty:
  - **Day-to-day swings** in conversion.
  - **The seasonal baseline itself.** One year is a weak guide to the normal seasonal lift, because the strength of the summer launch varies from year to year.
  - **Measurement.** A faster site can change the session count itself. Fewer visitors leave before the analytics script loads, so more short sessions get recorded. This inflates the denominator and could hide a real gain in orders. The effect is probably small, but it is a reason to also compare orders per day, adjusted for season, once last year's order counts are available.

Taken together, a CDN effect of a couple of tenths of a point in either direction cannot be excluded. That is roughly ±7% of conversion, or about 400 orders a fortnight (0.2 points × 210,000 sessions). The honest conclusion is that there is **no detectable conversion effect**. That is not the same as proof that there is no effect.

## What is a second worth?

These data do not support a per-second figure, for three reasons:

1. **The observed 0.2 points is seasonal.** After removing the seasonal lift, the change attributable to speed is about zero, with wide uncertainty. Dividing that by 1.1 seconds gives a number that is neither credible nor useful.
2. **One before/after pair cannot reveal a rate.** We have a single change in speed and a single change in conversion. We cannot tell whether the relationship is linear or has diminishing returns. Going from 3.2 s to 2.1 s may matter quite differently from going from 2.1 s to 1.1 s.
3. **The choice of speed metric is arbitrary.** The median improved by 1.1 seconds and the 95th percentile by 2.7 seconds. Dividing by one or the other gives different "per-second" values from the same data.

Conversion is also only one part of what speed is worth. A faster site can raise average order value, encourage repeat visits and improve search ranking, which brings in more sessions. None of these has been measured here. The data request in step 4 covers the first two, and step 5 covers value that does not depend on conversion at all.

## Next steps

1. **Run a controlled test to measure the value of speed.** Measure conversion, average order value and revenue per session, not conversion alone. Either of two designs removes seasonality and gives a defensible effect per second:
   - **Preferred:** roll out a specific speed improvement to a random share of traffic and compare it with the rest.
   - **Alternative:** add a small, controlled delay for a random share of traffic. This gives a cleaner reading on the value of speed, but it costs revenue while it runs, so stakeholders should agree to it in advance.
2. **Use the post-migration real-user monitoring data, and design around its main bias.** Simply comparing fast sessions with slow ones is misleading. Fast sessions come disproportionately from newer devices and better connections, and those customers convert differently anyway.
   - **Main design:** compare segments (device type, region, connection type) where the CDN cut load times the most against segments where it changed little, before and after 1 June. Seasonality affects both groups, so the difference between them isolates the speed effect much better.
   - **Controls:** control for traffic source and product category.
   - **Strength of evidence:** this is weaker than a test but quicker to produce.
3. **Do not use a points-per-second figure in business cases** until step 1 or step 2 produces one.
4. **Pull fuller data for both years.**
   - **Last year, same weeks:** unrounded conversion rates, session counts, order counts and bounce rate. These will tighten the seasonal comparison, allow orders per day and engagement to be adjusted for season, and show how much of this year's 5% session rise is normal.
   - **Both years:** average order value and revenue per session, so that "worth" can be judged on more than conversion.
   - **This year, before and after 1 June:** load times broken down by device, page type and region, to confirm that the speed gain is like for like rather than a shift in traffic mix.
   - **Ongoing:** keep monitoring load times weekly through the summer to confirm that the gains hold as traffic grows.
5. **Value the CDN on its other merits as well.** These include hosting and bandwidth costs, reliability and search ranking. None of them depends on a measurable conversion lift.

## Conclusion

The CDN migration made the site about a third faster, at both the median and the 95th percentile. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, but it rose by the same amount (to the precision available) at the same point last year because of the summer range launch. This holds whether the seasonal lift is treated as fixed or proportional. There is no evidence yet that the faster site improved conversion, but the data are too imprecise to rule out an effect of roughly ±7% either way. The value of a second of load time needs to be measured with a controlled test, across conversion, order value and revenue per session. It cannot be inferred from this before/after comparison.
